newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Denmark could not accept 3rd pillar transfer.
newsitem.headline: Denmark could not accept 3rd pillar transfer.

text.p: Denmark would not be able to agree to a transfer of policy areas from the European Union's third pillar to its first pillar, the country's chief negotiator at the IGC said on Tuesday.

Niels Ersboell said Denmark would not block a possible move of justice and home affairs from intergovernmental cooperation to traditional Community decision-making procedures, but said the country would then not be able to take part.
In effect, that would mean that Denmark would need to opt out if a transfer of such policies is agreed at the inter-governmental conference.
He said Denmark would then need to negotiate "a complicated system" with the other member states under which it could continue to participate in the cooperation.
However, Ersboell stressed that Denmark did not wish for such an outcome and that the third pillar could be made to work better in its existing framework.

"We obviously try to avoid that situation and do our best to demonstrate that it does not necessarily have to be the only way out," Ersboell told reporters after Tuesday's IGC meeting, which discussed third pillar issues.
The reason for Denmark's stance is that it has promised Danes not to accept issues being moved from the inter-governmental field unless this were approved in a new referendum.

Ersboell said the EU's present membership composition should not be split on "purely legal questions if we can get agreement on substance" and that from the perspective of eastern enlargement it was important to maintain the 15 member states as a group.
"We want to put the reality and action in front of a fairly ideological debate on whether it should be Community-oriented or whether it should be intergovernmental," he said.
Ersboell said Denmark believed progress could be made within the present system. "We agree that intergovernmental cooperation needs to be improved enormously," he said.
For example, the Commission could be much more active, he said. "The Commission can do much more if they wish," he said.
But, he said, for Denmark it was essential to have a strong role for the national parliament.
On Third Pillar issues, there is widespread agreement in the EU that the current system, where decisions are taken inter-governmentally, is not doing enough.
EU leaders, however, are keen to change this, seeing the EU actions on crime and immigration as playing a direct role in making the bloc more meaningful to its citizens.

Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring has said that the new treaty would keep the inter-governmental nature of the Third Pillar, but that some Community decision-making procedures would have to be adopted.

The chairman of the IGC group, Noel Dorr, said delegations which had problems with "Communitarisation" of third pillar issues were willing to go far on substance, arguing that much could be done under the present system.
Others, however, felt strongly that the present system was not working well and that it was important to move as far as possible to Community proceedings.
